title: Salary and the cooperative arrangement in the Basin Street Six
summary: Jones earned $100 a week against a scale near $56, as the only non-owner of a cooperative band, with Joe Rodas handling the mic.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Daniel Raposo. He died. Yeah. Anyway, uh, the, uh, I was always wondering about the salary with the Basin Street Six, how the financial arrangements were, who the lead it was, how the all that arranged things.

It was, uh, I went on the Basin Street Six, and it was a terrific salary at that time. I was making a hundred dollars a week. It's 1953, huh? 52, 53, I guess. When, uh, when, uh, scale, when musicians was only about fifty-eight dollars a week, fifty-six dollars a week. And I was the lowest paid dialing band. I was not one of the, uh, cooperative owners. The rest of the band was, it was a cooperative band. And, uh, it was kind of, uh, how can you say, whoever hollered the loudest got the tone played he wanted. But mostly Joe Rodas handled the mic. After George left the band, Joe handled the microphone. Uh-huh. And, needless to say, the guy with the mic in his hand, if he calls a song, it usually gets played. But, uh, there would be some discussion, sometimes, in, uh, some pretty loud language as to what would be played. But, uh, the continuity was usually pretty good on the band. Uh, I got the job done. It's a good show band. Good show band. And not that bad a Dixie Man band, either.
